title: Classes, Objects & Idiomatic Python
sub: Model hosts, ports and networks as types, then use dunder methods, dataclasses, generators, decorators and context managers
goals: Write classes with attributes, methods, properties, class methods and static methods
Make your own objects behave like built-ins with dunder methods such as __repr__, __eq__, __len__, __iter__ and __contains__
Choose between a plain class, a dataclass, an Enum and inheritance or composition for a given model
Build lazy generator pipelines that mirror shell pipelines
Write decorators and context managers, with and without arguments
Read and write basic type hints, including Optional values and Protocols
Assemble netmodel.py, the object model for the netkit capstone

blocks.text: So far your programs have been functions acting on lists and dicts. That works until the same facts travel together everywhere: an IP address, a name, a set of scan results, the rules for what counts as valid. A **class** bundles that data with the functions that understand it, and Python's special method names let your objects plug into `for` loops, `len()`, `in`, `sorted()` and `with` like the built-in types do. This chapter teaches classes from the ground up, then the idioms that make Python code short: dataclasses, enums, generators, decorators and context managers. You will model hosts, ports, subnets and an inventory, which become the core of `netkit`.

Make `~/lab/oop/` and open it in PyCharm. Type each example into a file or the Python Console (Tool Windows, Python Console) and change it. Objects are easiest to understand by poking at them: call `vars(obj)`, `type(obj)`, `dir(obj)` and `help(Class)` on everything.
Objects, classes and instances

Everything in Python is already an object: `"text"`, `42`, a function, a module. An object has an **identity** (where it lives), a **type** (what it is) and a **value** with attributes and methods. A **class** is the blueprint for a type, and an **instance** is one object built from it.

blocks.code:
class Host:
    count = 0                          # class attribute: one copy, shared by every instance

    def __init__(self, ip, name=""):   # runs when you call Host(...)
        self.ip = ip                   # instance attributes: one set per object
        self.name = name
        Host.count += 1

    def ping_command(self):
        return f"ping -c 3 {self.ip}"

a = Host("192.168.1.1", "router")
b = Host("192.168.1.20")
print(a.ping_command())
print(Host.ping_command(b))            # this is exactly what b.ping_command() does
print(Host.count, a.count, b.count)
print(vars(a))
print(type(a).__name__, isinstance(a, Host), a is b, a == Host("192.168.1.1"))
blocks.out:
ping -c 3 192.168.1.1
ping -c 3 192.168.1.20
2 2 2
{'ip': '192.168.1.1', 'name': 'router'}
Host True False False

blocks.text: Three mechanisms are visible in that output.

items.text: **`Host(...)` makes the object, then calls `__init__`.** `__init__` is not the constructor itself but the initializer: the new empty object already exists and arrives as `self`.

**`self` is just the first parameter.** `a.ping_command()` is translated to `Host.ping_command(a)`: Python looks the function up on the class and passes the instance as the first argument. The name `self` is a convention; the position is the rule.

**Attribute lookup walks upward.** `a.count` first looks in the instance's own dictionary (`vars(a)`), does not find `count`, then looks in the class, and finds it there. Assigning through the instance creates a new instance attribute and leaves the class attribute alone.

blocks.code:
class Host:
    count = 0
    def __init__(self, ip):
        self.ip = ip
        Host.count += 1

a, b = Host("192.0.2.1"), Host("192.0.2.2")
a.count = 99                           # creates an instance attribute that shadows the class one
print(Host.count, a.count, b.count)
print("count" in vars(a), "count" in vars(b))

blocks.text: By default `a == Host("192.168.1.1")` is False even though both have the same data: `==` on a plain class compares identity. The dunder section below shows how to change that.

blocks.title: A mutable class attribute is shared state

blocks.text: `class Host: ports = []` creates **one** list that every instance appends to. Create mutable attributes in `__init__` (`self.ports = []`), where each instance gets its own.

blocks.name: class (Python)
blocks.sum: Define a new type with attributes and methods.

how.text: Executing a `class` statement runs its indented body once, collects the names defined there (the class attributes and the functions) into a namespace, and creates a **type object** from it that is bound to `Name`. Calling `Name(args)` creates an instance, then calls `Name.__init__(instance, args)`. Methods are ordinary functions stored on the class; accessing one through an instance binds the instance as the first argument. Names starting with one underscore (`_cache`) are a convention for "internal"; Python does not enforce it. A class with no explicit base inherits from `object`.

examples.desc: A class, an instance and what they hold
Turn lines from a pipe into objects and print a summary

gotchas: Forgetting `self` in a method definition gives `TypeError: f() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given`: Python passed the instance and the function had nowhere to put it.

blocks.name: __init__
blocks.sum: Initialize a new instance; called right after the object is created.

how.text: `Name(...)` first calls `Name.__new__` (almost always the inherited one, which allocates an empty object), then `__init__` with that object as `self` and your arguments. It must return `None`. Put validation here and raise `ValueError` for bad input so that an invalid object can never exist. If a subclass defines `__init__`, it should call `super().__init__(...)` to initialize the parent's part.

examples.desc: Validate while building
Reject bad input lines while loading, with the line number on stderr

gotchas: Never give `__init__` a mutable default such as `def __init__(self, ports=[])`; the one list is shared by all instances. Use `ports=None` and `self.ports = list(ports or ())`.

blocks.name: object
blocks.sum: The base class of every class; supplies default behavior for ==, repr, hash and more.
blocks.syntax: class Name(object) is the same as class Name

how.text: Every class inherits from `object`, which provides `__eq__` (identity), `__hash__` (based on identity), `__repr__` (`<__main__.Host object at 0x...>`), `__str__` (calls repr), `__init__` (does nothing), `__setattr__` and `__getattribute__`. Overriding a method in your class replaces the default for your instances only. `dir(obj)` lists all of them.

examples.desc: What a bare instance gives you
examples.code:
class Empty: pass
e = Empty()
print(type(e).__mro__[-1].__name__, e == Empty(), hasattr(e, "__repr__"))
print(repr(e).startswith("<__main__.Empty object at 0x"))

examples.desc: Count the default methods every object has
examples.code: python3 -c 'print(len(dir(object())))'

blocks.text: Methods: instance, class and static
A method is a function stored on a class. Three flavors differ in what Python passes as the first argument.

head: Kind
Declared with
First argument
Use it for
rows: behavior that reads or changes one object
alternative constructors, and anything that should work for subclasses too
a utility that belongs to the class's topic but needs neither the class nor an instance

blocks.text: The last line is the reason for `@classmethod`: because `cls` is whatever class the method was called on, subclasses get their own type back from the same constructor. A hard-coded `Host(...)` inside the method would always return a `Host`.

blocks.name: @classmethod
blocks.sum: Declare a method that receives the class instead of an instance.

how.text: The decorator wraps the function so that accessing it on a class or an instance passes the class as the first argument. Its main use is the **alternative constructor** pattern: `Host.from_line(...)`, `Port.parse("22/tcp")`, `datetime.fromisoformat(...)`. Because it receives `cls`, `cls(...)` creates an instance of the right subclass.

examples.desc: Alternative constructor
Parse port specs from the shell into objects and list them

blocks.name: @staticmethod
blocks.sum: Declare a plain function that lives in a class's namespace.

how.text: The function receives only the arguments you pass: no `self`, no `cls`. It could be a module-level function; placing it in the class documents that it belongs with the type and lets subclasses override it. If a static method needs the class, make it a class method instead.

examples.desc: A utility grouped with its class
Normalize MAC addresses read from a pipe

blocks.text: Properties: computed and validated attributes

A **property** looks like an attribute to the caller but runs code. Start with a plain attribute (the simplest thing that works); turn it into a property later if you need validation or a computed value, without changing any calling code.

The stored value lives in `_mtu` (leading underscore: "internal"), and the public name `mtu` is the property. `1500.0` passed the range check, which shows that a validator should also care about type if that matters to you. The read-only property raises `AttributeError` on assignment because it has no setter.

blocks.name: @property
blocks.sum: Expose a method as an attribute, optionally with a setter that validates.
blocks.syntax: @property  def x(self): ...    then    @x.setter  def x(self, value): ...

how.text: `property` is a **descriptor**: an object stored on the class whose `__get__` runs when you read `obj.x` and whose `__set__` runs when you assign. The getter is called with no arguments each time, so the value is recomputed on every access (use `functools.cached_property` to compute once). Without a setter the attribute is read-only. Use properties for validation, computed values (`net.broadcast`) and renaming without breaking callers; do not write getters and setters for every attribute as in Java.

examples.desc: A computed read-only attribute
Compute usable hosts for each prefix length read from stdin

gotchas: Inside the getter, `return self.mtu` calls the property again and recurses forever. Store the value under another name (`self._mtu`).

blocks.text: Dunder methods: making objects behave like built-ins

Methods whose names begin and end with two underscores ("dunder" methods, from "double underscore") are hooks. You do not call them; Python calls them when you use syntax or built-in functions. Defining the right few makes your class feel native.

head: You write
Python calls
So that
rows: developers can see an unambiguous form
equality means equal data, not the same object
objects can be set members and dict keys
the object can be looped over
the object can be called like a function

blocks.text: The block below defines a `Subnet` with most of them and uses each one by syntax alone.
Things worth noticing:

items.text: **`__repr__` vs `__str__`.** `repr` is for debugging and should look like code that rebuilds the object, which is why a list of objects shows their `repr`. If you define only one, define `__repr__`; `str` falls back to it.

**`__eq__` and `__hash__` travel together.** Python sets `__hash__` to `None` when you define `__eq__` alone, which makes the class unhashable. Equal objects must have equal hashes, so hash exactly the data you compare.
**Only `__lt__` is needed for `sorted`.** `sorted` and `min`/`max` use `<`. To get all six comparison operators from one method, add `@functools.total_ordering`, or use a dataclass with `order=True`.
**`__iter__` + `__getitem__`.** `for` uses `__iter__`. If a class has only `__getitem__` with integer indexes, Python still iterates it by trying 0, 1, 2 until `IndexError`, an older protocol.
**Return `NotImplemented`, not `False`,** from `__eq__` or `__lt__` when the other object is a type you do not handle; Python then tries the reflected operation on the other side.

blocks.name: __repr__
blocks.sum: Return the unambiguous developer form of an object.

how.text: Called by `repr(obj)`, by the interactive prompt, by debuggers, and when the object appears inside a list, dict or traceback. The convention is a string that looks like the constructor call, `Port(22, 'tcp')`, or `<...>` when that is impossible. Good reprs make failures readable: an assertion error or pytest diff that shows `Port(22, 'tcp')` beats `<Port object at 0x10a2b3c40>`. `str()` and f-strings use `__str__`, which falls back to `__repr__` when absent.

examples.desc: Readable debugging output
Dump objects as one repr per line for grep
examples.code:
python3 -c 'class P:
    def __init__(s, n): s.n = n
    def __repr__(s): return f"P({s.n})"
print(*[P(n) for n in (22, 80, 443)], sep="\n")' | grep -c 'P('

blocks.name: __str__
blocks.sum: Return the readable form of an object for users.

how.text: Called by `str(obj)`, `print(obj)` and `f"{obj}"`. It should be short and readable by someone who does not know your code. If it is missing, Python uses `__repr__`. Both must return a `str`, never print.

examples.desc: Different forms for different readers
Print objects the way a report column would show them
examples.code:
python3 -c 'class P:
    def __init__(s, n): s.n = n
    def __str__(s): return f"{s.n}/tcp"
print(*[P(n) for n in (22, 80)], sep="\n")' | sort -r

blocks.name: __eq__
blocks.sum: Define what == means for your objects.

how.text: `a == b` calls `a.__eq__(b)`. Return `NotImplemented` if `other` is a type you do not know, so Python can try `b.__eq__(a)` before falling back to identity. Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__` makes the class unhashable, because mutable data should not be used as a key; add `__hash__` only for objects you treat as immutable.

examples.desc: Compare by value
Count distinct ports from a stream using value equality through a list search

gotchas: `p not in list` uses `__eq__` and is O(n). For many objects define `__hash__` too and use a set.

blocks.name: __hash__
blocks.sum: Return an integer so the object can be a set member or dict key.

how.text: Sets and dicts store an object at a position computed from `hash(obj)` and then confirm with `==`, so the rule is: **objects that compare equal must have equal hashes**. The usual implementation hashes a tuple of the compared fields: `hash((self.ip, self.port))`. Only do this for objects that do not change after creation; if the fields change while the object sits in a set, it is lost. Dataclasses with `frozen=True` generate this for you.

examples.desc: Use your objects as dict keys
Deduplicate ports from stdin using a set of hashable objects
examples.code:
printf '22
80
22
' | python3 -c 'import sys; print(len({int(l) for l in sys.stdin}))'

blocks.name: __lt__
blocks.sum: Define ordering so objects work with sorted(), min() and max().

how.text: `sorted()` and `min()`/`max()` only use `<`. Define `__lt__` and the other comparisons are not available automatically: `a > b` works because Python tries the reflected `b < a`, but `a <= b` does not. Decorate the class with `functools.total_ordering` (needs `__eq__` and one ordering method) or use `@dataclass(order=True)` to get all of them.

examples.desc: Sort objects by address
Sort IPv4 addresses numerically from a pipe (text sort would put 10 before 9)
examples.code:
printf '10.0.0.10
9.9.9.9
10.0.0.9
' | python3 -c 'import sys, ipaddress; print(*sorted((l.strip() for l in sys.stdin), key=ipaddress.ip_address), sep="
")'

blocks.name: __len__
blocks.sum: Give your object a length for len(), and truthiness when empty.

how.text: `len(obj)` calls it and requires a non-negative int no larger than `sys.maxsize`. If a class defines `__len__` but not `__bool__`, `bool(obj)` is `len(obj) != 0`, so empty containers are falsy. For an IPv6 /64 the true size overflows `len()`, so use `num_addresses` for those.

examples.desc: A collection with a size
Count the lines of a stream through a small collection class

blocks.name: __iter__
blocks.sum: Make an object usable in a for loop, list(), sorted() and unpacking.

how.text: `for x in obj` calls `iter(obj)`, which calls `obj.__iter__()`. It must return an **iterator**: an object with `__next__`. The simplest way is `return iter(self._items)`, or to write `__iter__` as a generator with `yield`. Returning a fresh iterator on every call means the collection can be looped over many times; an object that returns itself (`return self`) is a one-shot iterator.

examples.desc: A collection that can be looped over
Wrap a stream in an iterable class that sorts it

gotchas: `in` works on an object that only has `__iter__` by scanning it, which is O(n). Define `__contains__` when a faster test exists.

blocks.name: __next__
blocks.sum: Return the next item of an iterator, or raise StopIteration at the end.

how.text: An **iterator** has `__next__` (and `__iter__` returning itself). The `for` loop calls `__next__` repeatedly until it raises `StopIteration`. Writing an iterator class by hand is rarely necessary: a generator function gives you the same thing in a third of the code. The built-in `next(it, default)` calls this method.

examples.desc: A hand-written countdown iterator
Print a countdown iterator as a comma-separated list
examples.code:
python3 -c 'class C:
    def __init__(s, n): s.n = n
    def __iter__(s): return s
    def __next__(s):
        if s.n == 0: raise StopIteration
        s.n -= 1; return s.n
print(*C(4))' | tr ' ' ','

blocks.name: __getitem__
blocks.sum: Support obj[key], including indexes and slices.

how.text: `obj[k]` calls `obj.__getitem__(k)`. For sequence-like classes `k` is an int or a `slice` object (`obj[1:3]` passes `slice(1, 3)`); for mapping-like classes it is any key. Raise `KeyError` for a missing key and `IndexError` for a bad index, so callers can catch the standard exceptions. Define `__setitem__` and `__delitem__` for assignment and `del`.

examples.desc: Look up hosts by address
Resolve addresses from stdin through an indexable object

blocks.name: __contains__
blocks.sum: Define what the in operator means for your object.

how.text: `x in obj` calls `obj.__contains__(x)`. Without it Python falls back to `__iter__` (a scan) and then to `__getitem__`. Define it when you can answer faster or more meaningfully than a scan, as `Subnet` does with a bit comparison instead of generating every host. Return `False` for values of the wrong type unless a `TypeError` is more helpful.

examples.desc: Membership as a network test
Keep only the addresses that belong to a subnet
examples.code:
printf '192.168.1.9
10.0.0.1
192.168.1.200
' | python3 -c 'import sys, ipaddress
net = ipaddress.ip_network("192.168.1.0/24")
print(*[l.strip() for l in sys.stdin if ipaddress.ip_address(l.strip()) in net], sep="
")'

blocks.name: __enter__ and __exit__
blocks.sum: Make an object usable in a with statement with guaranteed cleanup.
blocks.syntax: def __enter__(self) -> value      def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) -> bool

how.text: `with obj as name:` calls `obj.__enter__()` and binds its return value to `name`. When the block ends, however it ends, Python calls `obj.__exit__(exc_type, exc, tb)`; the three arguments are all `None` after a normal finish and describe the exception otherwise. Returning a true value from `__exit__` **suppresses** the exception; returning `None` or `False` lets it continue. See the context managers section for the generator-based shortcut.

examples.desc: Cleanup runs on success and on error
examples.code:
class Session:
    def __enter__(self):
        print("open")
        return self
    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb):
        print("close", exc_type.__name__ if exc_type else "ok")
        return exc_type is KeyError          # suppress KeyError only
with Session():
    print("working")
with Session():
    {}["x"]
print("after the suppressed KeyError")
examples.out:
open
working
close ok
open
close KeyError
after the suppressed KeyError

examples.desc: Write to a temp file through a context manager and read it back in the shell
examples.code: python3 -c 'with open("/tmp/ctx_demo.txt", "w") as f: f.write("saved\n")' && cat /tmp/ctx_demo.txt && rm /tmp/ctx_demo.txt

blocks.name: __call__
blocks.sum: Make an instance callable like a function that remembers state.

how.text: `obj(args)` calls `type(obj).__call__(obj, args)`. It lets you build a function with configuration and memory without a closure: a rate limiter, a validator with settings, a decorator written as a class. `callable(obj)` is true for any object whose class defines it.

examples.desc: A validator configured once
examples.code:
class PortRange:
    def __init__(self, low, high): self.low, self.high = low, high
    def __call__(self, port): return self.low <= port <= self.high
unprivileged = PortRange(1024, 65535)
print(unprivileged(8080), unprivileged(22), callable(unprivileged))

examples.desc: Filter ports from stdin with a callable object
examples.code:
printf '22\n8080\n443\n' | python3 -c 'import sys
class R:
    def __init__(s, lo): s.lo = lo
    def __call__(s, p): return p >= s.lo
ok = R(1024)
print(*[l.strip() for l in sys.stdin if ok(int(l))])'

blocks.name: __add__
blocks.sum: Define the + operator (and, by the same pattern, - * / and others).

how.text: `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`; if that returns `NotImplemented` or does not exist, Python tries `b.__radd__(a)`, which is why `sum()` (which starts from `0 + x`) needs `__radd__` to handle the integer. Return a **new** object from `__add__`; `+=` uses `__iadd__` if present and otherwise falls back to `__add__`. Use operators only where the meaning is obvious: adding two packet counters is fine, adding two hosts is not.

examples.desc: A counter pair that adds element-wise
Total per-interface traffic from a stream of "rx tx" lines
examples.code:
printf '100 20\n5 1\n' | python3 -c 'import sys
class T:
    def __init__(s, rx, tx): s.rx, s.tx = rx, tx
    def __add__(s, o): return T(s.rx + o.rx, s.tx + o.tx)
rows = [T(*map(int, l.split())) for l in sys.stdin]
total = rows[0]
for r in rows[1:]: total = total + r
print(total.rx, total.tx)'

blocks.name: __bool__
blocks.sum: Decide whether an object is true in if, while and bool().

how.text: Python asks `__bool__` first, then `__len__` (non-zero is true), and treats any object that defines neither as true. Use it to make "empty" or "failed" results falsy so callers can write `if result:`. Keep it cheap and never raise from it.

examples.desc: A result that is falsy when it failed
Exit with a status derived from truthiness, usable in shell &&
examples.code:
python3 -c 'import sys
class R:
    def __bool__(s): return False
sys.exit(0 if R() else 1)' || echo "failed as designed"

blocks.name: __slots__
blocks.sum: Declare the only attributes instances may have, saving memory and catching typos.

how.text: Normally each instance carries a dict for its attributes. With `__slots__` Python reserves fixed storage for the named attributes instead, which shrinks each object and makes millions of small objects practical, and assigning any other name raises `AttributeError`. The cost is no `vars(obj)`, no weak references unless you add `"__weakref__"`, and care with inheritance. Dataclasses take `slots=True` (Python 3.10+) to generate it. Do not reach for it before you have measured a memory problem.

examples.desc: A typo becomes an error
Compare the size of a plain and a slotted object
examples.code:
python3 -c 'import sys
class A:
    def __init__(s): s.x = 1
class B:
    __slots__ = ("x",)
    def __init__(s): s.x = 1
print(sys.getsizeof(A()) + sys.getsizeof(A().__dict__) > sys.getsizeof(B()))'

blocks.text: Dataclasses
Classes that mostly hold data need the same boilerplate every time: `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`. The `dataclasses` module writes them for you from annotated fields.

blocks.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field, asdict, replace

@dataclass
class Port:
    number: int
    proto: str = "tcp"                       # a default makes the field optional

@dataclass
class Host:
    ip: str
    name: str = ""
    ports: list = field(default_factory=list)   # mutable defaults need a factory

p = Port(443)
print(p)
print(p == Port(443), p == Port(443, "udp"))
h = Host("192.168.1.1", "router")
h.ports.append(p)
print(h)
print(asdict(h))
print(replace(h, name="gateway"))
print(Host("10.0.0.1").ports is Host("10.0.0.2").ports)
blocks.out:
Port(number=443, proto='tcp')
True False
Host(ip='192.168.1.1', name='router', ports=[Port(number=443, proto='tcp')])
{'ip': '192.168.1.1', 'name': 'router', 'ports': [{'number': 443, 'proto': 'tcp'}]}
Host(ip='192.168.1.1', name='gateway', ports=[Port(number=443, proto='tcp')])
False

blocks.text: `@dataclass` read the annotations and generated `__init__(self, number, proto="tcp")`, a `__repr__` that lists the fields, and `__eq__` that compares them as a tuple. `field(default_factory=list)` creates a fresh list per instance, which sidesteps the shared-default trap (a plain `ports: list = []` is rejected with a `ValueError`). Annotations are required, but the types are not enforced: `Port("x")` is accepted.
Options on the decorator change what is generated:

head: Option
Effect
Typical use
rows: instances cannot be changed; `__hash__` is generated
values you use as dict keys or set members: addresses, ports
all fields must be passed by name (3.10+)
objects with identity, such as a connection

blocks.out:
[Port(number=22, proto='tcp'), Port(number=53, proto='udp'), Port(number=443, proto='tcp')]
ssh
FrozenInstanceError
port out of range: 70000

blocks.text: `__post_init__` is where validation goes. With `frozen=True` assignment raises `FrozenInstanceError` (a subclass of `AttributeError`), and the generated `__hash__` lets the ports serve as dictionary keys.

**When to use what?** A dataclass is the default for "a record with named fields". Use `NamedTuple` or `collections.namedtuple` when you want something tuple-like and immutable that unpacks, a plain class when behavior dominates and the state is private, a dict only for data of unknown shape (JSON you have not parsed yet).

blocks.name: @dataclass
blocks.sum: Generate __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and optionally ordering and hashing from annotated fields.
blocks.syntax: @dataclass(frozen=False, order=False, slots=False, kw_only=False)   class C: field: type = default

how.text: The decorator inspects the class annotations in order and writes the special methods. A field with a default must come after fields without one (like function parameters). The mutable-default check rejects `list`, `dict` and `set` defaults; use `field(default_factory=...)`. Helper functions: `asdict(obj)` and `astuple(obj)` convert recursively, `replace(obj, name=value)` builds a modified copy, `fields(cls)` lists the field objects. Type annotations are for readers and tools and are not checked at run time.

examples.desc: A record with a default
examples.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class Result:
    host: str
    port: int
    open: bool = False
r = Result("192.0.2.1", 22)
print(r, r == Result("192.0.2.1", 22, False))

examples.desc: Turn CSV lines into records and print them as JSON for jq or a file
examples.code:
printf 'web,80\ndb,5432\n' | python3 -c 'import sys, json
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict
@dataclass
class Svc:
    name: str
    port: int
rows = [Svc(n, int(p)) for n, p in (l.strip().split(",") for l in sys.stdin)]
print(json.dumps([asdict(r) for r in rows]))'

blocks.name: dataclasses.field()
blocks.sum: Customize one dataclass field: default factory, exclusion from repr, compare or init.

how.text: `default_factory` is called with no arguments for every new instance and is how you give each object its own list, dict or set. `repr=False` hides a noisy field from the display, `compare=False` removes it from `==` and ordering (useful for a cache or a note), and `init=False` means the field is not an `__init__` parameter and is set elsewhere, for example in `__post_init__`.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
@dataclass
class Host:
    ip: str
    notes: list = field(default_factory=list, compare=False, repr=False)
a, b = Host("192.0.2.1"), Host("192.0.2.1")
a.notes.append("seen on vlan 20")
print(a == b, a, b.notes)

blocks.text: Inheritance, polymorphism and composition

**Inheritance** creates a new class that starts with everything a parent class has, then adds or replaces behavior. **Polymorphism** means code that calls the same method on different objects and gets behavior that fits each one.

blocks.out:
192.168.1.99: generic device
gw: router, WAN 203.0.113.2
nas: server
True False
['Router', 'Device', 'object']

blocks.text: `super()` returns a proxy that finds the next class in the **method resolution order** (MRO), shown on the last line. With a single parent it is simply "the parent", and with several parents the MRO decides the order consistently. The `isinstance` function is True for the class and all its ancestors.
Abstract base classes

An **abstract base class** declares methods that every subclass must provide. Python refuses to create an instance until all abstract methods are implemented, which turns a forgotten method into an immediate error instead of a failure deep in a run.

blocks.out:
Can't instantiate abstract class Probe without an implementation for abstract method 'check'
{22: True, 80: False, 443: True}

blocks.text: A `FakeProbe` that answers from a set is also how you test scanning code without touching the network: swap the real probe for the fake one.
Composition: has-a instead of is-a

Inheritance couples a subclass to every detail of its parent. **Composition** builds a bigger object from smaller ones and talks to them through their methods. The test: say "a Router **is a** Device" aloud; if it is true for all time, inheritance is reasonable. "A Scanner **has a** Probe" is composition, and means you can supply a different probe without touching the scanner.

`FakeProbe` does not inherit from anything, yet `Scanner` accepts it. That is **duck typing**: if it has a `check(host, port)` method, it works. `typing.Protocol` (type hints section) lets you write that expectation down for tools to verify.

head: Question
Inheritance
Composition
rows: changes in the parent break children
more small classes to wire together
you extend a stable base class, or define an interface with `ABC`
you combine behaviors or need testability

blocks.name: super()
blocks.sum: Call a method of the next class in the method resolution order.

how.text: Inside a method, `super()` finds the class after the current one in `type(self).__mro__` and returns an object whose attribute lookups start there, bound to `self`. The most common use is `super().__init__(...)` so the parent initializes its attributes, and `super().method()` to extend rather than replace behavior. With multiple inheritance each class calls `super()` once and the MRO ensures every parent runs once.

examples.desc: Extend, do not replace
Print the order in which Python resolves a method, one class per line
examples.code:
python3 -c 'class A: pass
class B(A): pass
print(*[c.__name__ for c in B.__mro__], sep="\n")'

gotchas: Forgetting `super().__init__()` in a subclass leaves the parent's attributes unset, and the error shows up later as `AttributeError`.

blocks.name: abc.ABC
blocks.sum: Base class for defining an interface with @abstractmethod methods that subclasses must implement.

how.text: A class whose metaclass is `ABCMeta` (what inheriting from `ABC` gives you) records its abstract methods. Calling the class raises `TypeError` while any abstract method remains unimplemented. The abstract method can contain a docstring or default code that subclasses reach through `super()`. Use ABCs sparingly: when duck typing or a `Protocol` is enough, an ABC adds ceremony.

blocks.text: Enums

A fixed set of named values (a port state, a protocol, a log level) should be an **enum**, not loose strings. A typo such as `"opne"` is silently a different string; `PortState.OPNE` is an immediate `AttributeError`.

blocks.code:
from enum import Enum, IntEnum, auto

class PortState(Enum):
    OPEN = "open"
    CLOSED = "closed"
    FILTERED = "filtered"

class Proto(IntEnum):                         # compares and sorts as an int
    ICMP = 1
    TCP = 6
    UDP = 17

class Level(Enum):
    LOW = auto()                              # let Python number them
    HIGH = auto()

print(PortState.OPEN, repr(PortState.OPEN))
print(PortState("closed"), PortState["FILTERED"], PortState.OPEN.value)
print([s.name for s in PortState])
print(PortState.OPEN is PortState("open"), PortState.OPEN == "open")
print(Proto.TCP == 6, sorted(Proto, reverse=True)[0].name, Level.HIGH.value)
try:
    PortState("opne")
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
blocks.out:
PortState.OPEN <PortState.OPEN: 'open'>
PortState.CLOSED PortState.FILTERED open
['OPEN', 'CLOSED', 'FILTERED']
True False
True UDP 2
'opne' is not a valid PortState

blocks.text: Members are singletons, so compare with `is` or `==`. A plain `Enum` member does not equal its value (`PortState.OPEN == "open"` is False), which prevents mixing; `IntEnum` is the compatibility choice for numbers that must behave like ints, such as protocol numbers. Looking up by value (`PortState("closed")`) raises `ValueError` for unknown input, which makes enums a good parser for fixed vocabularies.

blocks.name: enum.Enum
blocks.sum: Define a fixed set of named constants.
blocks.syntax: class Name(Enum): MEMBER = value   |   Name(value)   |   Name["MEMBER"]   |   Name.MEMBER.name / .value

how.text: Each assignment in the class body becomes a singleton member with `name` and `value` attributes. Iterating the class yields members in definition order. `Name(value)` looks up by value and raises `ValueError`; `Name["MEMBER"]` looks up by name and raises `KeyError`. Subclasses `IntEnum` and `StrEnum` (3.11+) also compare equal to their raw values, and `Flag` supports combining members with `|`.

examples.desc: States as members
examples.code:
from enum import Enum
class State(Enum):
    UP = "up"
    DOWN = "down"
print(State("up"), State.DOWN.name, list(State))

blocks.text: Iterators and generators

An **iterator** produces items one at a time and remembers where it is. An **iterable** is anything you can get an iterator from (`iter(x)`): lists, files, dicts, strings, your own classes with `__iter__`. A `for` loop is: call `iter()`, call `next()` until `StopIteration`.

A **generator function** is a function containing `yield`. Calling it does not run the body; it returns a generator object, which is an iterator. Each `next()` resumes the function after the last `yield`, with all its local variables intact, until the next `yield`.

blocks.code:
def countdown(n):
    print("start")
    while n > 0:
        yield n                 # hand a value out, pause here
        n -= 1
    print("done")

gen = countdown(3)
print("created, nothing printed yet")
print(next(gen))
print(next(gen))
print(list(gen))                # consumes the rest
print(list(gen))                # exhausted: generators are one-shot
blocks.out:
created, nothing printed yet
start
3
2
done
[1]
[]

blocks.text: Why bother? **Memory and time.** `sum(x * x for x in range(10_000_000))` never builds a ten-million-item list. And **composition**: generators are the Python form of a shell pipeline. Each stage is a small function that pulls from the previous one and yields to the next, nothing is read until the last stage asks for it, and a `head`-like stop at the end stops the reading at the start.

blocks.code:
shell:   cat access.log  |  grep ' 404 '  |  awk '{print $1}'  |  sort  |  uniq -c  |  sort -rn  |  head -2

  python:  read_lines(fh) ─▶ only_status(404) ─▶ client_ip ─▶ Counter ─▶ .most_common(3)
              ⟪c:generator⟫        ⟪c:generator⟫       ⟪c:generator⟫      ⟪y:consumer⟫     ⟪y:consumer⟫

import io
from collections import Counter

LOG = io.StringIO('''45.33.32.156 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 404 512
198.51.100.8 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:14:15 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 7625
45.33.32.156 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:14:42 +0000] "GET /.env HTTP/1.1" 404 365
this line is damaged
172.16.5.9 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:15:02 +0000] "GET /x HTTP/1.1" 404 90
45.33.32.156 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:15:09 +0000] "POST /login HTTP/1.1" 401 210
''')

def read_lines(fh):                         # cat
    for line in fh:
        yield line.rstrip("\n")

def parse(lines):                           # split into fields, drop damaged lines
    for line in lines:
        parts = line.split('"')
        if len(parts) < 3:
            continue
        ip = line.split()[0]
        status = int(parts[2].split()[0])
        yield {"ip": ip, "status": status, "request": parts[1]}

def only_status(records, code):             # grep
    return (r for r in records if r["status"] == code)

def field(records, name):                   # awk '{print $1}'
    return (r[name] for r in records)

top = Counter(field(only_status(parse(read_lines(LOG)), 404), "ip")).most_common(2)   # sort | uniq -c | head
print(top)

blocks.text: Each stage is a few lines, testable alone, and the data flows lazily: `Counter` pulls one record at a time through all four stages. Note `only_status` and `field` use **generator expressions** (a comprehension in parentheses), which are generators without `def`.
Watching the laziness makes it concrete:

blocks.code:
def noisy(name, source):
    for item in source:
        print(f"  {name} sees {item}")
        yield item

nums = noisy("A", range(1, 5))
evens = noisy("B", (n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0))
first = next(evens)
print("first even:", first)
blocks.out:
A sees 1
  A sees 2
  B sees 2
first even: 2

blocks.text: Only items 1 and 2 were read; 3 and 4 were never touched. That is what lets a generator pipeline process a 20 GB log in constant memory, or read endlessly from `tail -f`.
**`yield from`** delegates to another iterable and keeps the code flat:

blocks.name: yield (Python)
blocks.sum: Turn a function into a generator that produces values one at a time.
blocks.syntax: def f(...): ... yield value ...      yield from iterable

how.text: A function containing `yield` is compiled as a generator function: calling it returns a generator object without running any of its body. `next(gen)` runs until the next `yield`, returns that value and freezes the frame, keeping local variables and the position. When the function returns, `StopIteration` is raised, which ends a `for` loop. Generators are single-pass; call the function again for a fresh one. `yield from x` yields every item of `x` and returns the sub-generator's return value. `gen.send(v)` and `gen.close()` allow two-way communication and early shutdown.

examples.desc: Lazy production
A generator as one stage of a real shell pipeline

gotchas: A generator can be consumed only once. `len(gen)` does not work, and `list(gen)` twice returns an empty list the second time.

blocks.text: Decorators

Functions are objects: you can store them in variables, pass them as arguments and return them from other functions. A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement, usually a wrapper that adds behavior before and after. The `@name` line above a `def` is shorthand for `f = name(f)`.

blocks.out:
5000050000
sum_to | Add the numbers 1..n.
True True

blocks.text: Three details matter. The wrapper accepts any combination of positional and keyword arguments (the `*args` and `kwargs` pair in its signature), so it fits any function. It **returns** what the function returned. And `functools.wraps` copies `__name__`, `__doc__` and other metadata onto the wrapper; without it, every decorated function would be named `wrapper` in tracebacks, logs and `help()`.
Decorators with arguments

`@retry(times=3)` calls `retry(times=3)` first, and that call must return the actual decorator. So there are three nested layers: the factory (takes the settings), the decorator (takes the function), the wrapper (takes the call).

blocks.out:
attempt 1/3 failed: refused
attempt 2/3 failed: refused
payload

blocks.text: The retry loop from [Errors and debugging](#py-errors), packaged so any function can use it with one line. Decorators are also how frameworks register things (`@app.route`, `@pytest.fixture`, `@property`), so you will read them everywhere even if you write few.

blocks.title: A decorator with arguments, layer by layer

tokens.exp: evaluated first: calls the factory, which returns decorator
the function that decorator receives and wraps
actually calls wrapper, which calls the original up to 3 times

blocks.name: functools.wraps
blocks.sum: Make a wrapper function look like the function it wraps.

how.text: `wraps` is itself a decorator that copies `__name__`, `__qualname__`, `__doc__`, `__module__` and `__dict__` from the wrapped function onto the wrapper and sets `wrapper.__wrapped__ = func`. Debuggers, `help()`, pytest, logging and `inspect.signature` rely on that metadata. Always use it in decorators you write.

examples.desc: Without wraps the name is lost
Show the wrapped function's name in a log line for grep

blocks.text: Context managers

`with` guarantees cleanup, and you can write your own cleanup logic in two ways. The class form uses `__enter__` and `__exit__` (shown in the dunder section). The function form uses a generator and `contextlib.contextmanager`: code before `yield` is the setup, the yielded value is what `as` receives, and code after `yield` is the cleanup, put in `finally` so it also runs on errors.

blocks.out:
begin scan
inside: SCAN
end scan
begin probe
end probe
caught after cleanup: lost
'this is not shown\n'

blocks.text: The error still reached the caller, but `end probe` printed first. `redirect_stdout` is itself a context manager from the standard library, and `captured` nests it. In tests this pattern replaces printing with something you can assert on.

blocks.name: contextlib.contextmanager
blocks.sum: Build a context manager from a generator function with one yield.
blocks.syntax: @contextlib.contextmanager  def name(args): setup; try: yield value; finally: cleanup

how.text: The decorator turns the generator into an object with `__enter__` and `__exit__`. `__enter__` runs the generator to the `yield` and returns the yielded value. `__exit__` resumes it: after a normal block it just continues, and after an exception it **throws the exception into the generator at the yield**. Wrap the `yield` in `try/finally` so cleanup runs on errors, and catch the exception yourself if you want to suppress it.

examples.desc: Temporarily change a setting
Time a block and report on stderr so the pipeline output stays clean
examples.code:
seq 1 3 | python3 -c 'import sys, time, contextlib
@contextlib.contextmanager
def timer():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    try: yield
    finally: print("done", file=sys.stderr)
with timer():
    print(sum(int(l) for l in sys.stdin))'

blocks.text: Type hints

**Annotations** attach a type to a variable, parameter or return value. Python stores them and does nothing else; they are documentation that editors and checkers (PyCharm's inspections, `mypy`, `pyright`) turn into warnings before you run the code.
The last call passed a number as the host and a string as the ports, and Python executed it anyway. Type hints are checked by tools, not by the interpreter.

head: Hint
Meaning
Notes
rows: a function taking a str and returning bool
what a generator yields, what you can loop over

blocks.text: **`Optional` values** are the hint you will write most: a function that may return nothing is `-> str | None`, and the checker then forces callers to handle `None` before using the result. That catches the classic `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...` before it happens.
**`Protocol`** writes down duck typing. Any class with matching methods satisfies it, with no inheritance:

A type checker accepts `FakeProbe` for `Probe` because it has the right method; at run time nothing differs. Start by hinting function signatures and dataclass fields, where the benefit is highest, and let PyCharm's yellow underlines guide you. You do not need to annotate every local variable.

blocks.name: type hints
blocks.sum: Annotate parameters, returns and variables with expected types for editors and checkers.
blocks.syntax: def f(x: int, y: str = "a") -> bool: ...      name: list[str] = []      from typing import Protocol, Any

how.text: Annotations are evaluated and stored in `__annotations__`; the interpreter never enforces them. Tools read them to find mistakes, to complete code and to document intent. Dataclasses and `typing.NamedTuple` use them to know their fields, so there the annotation does matter at run time. Use built-in generics (`list[int]`) on Python 3.9+ and `X | None` on 3.10+.

examples.desc: Hints are metadata
Run a type checker over a script in a pipeline (after pip install mypy in a venv)
examples.code: python3 -m mypy hello.py 2>&1 | tail -n 1

gotchas: `def f(items: list = [])` still has the mutable default problem; hints do not change that.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Mutable class attributes** (`ports = []` in the class body). Create them in `__init__` or with `field(default_factory=list)`.
**Forgetting `self`** in a method signature, or inside the method (`ip` instead of `self.ip`: `NameError`).
**Defining `__eq__` without `__hash__`** and then being surprised that the object is unhashable.
**Returning `None` from `__repr__` or printing inside it.** It must return a `str`.
**Deep inheritance for code reuse.** Three levels of subclasses is a signal to switch to composition.
**Generators used twice.** The second pass is empty. Store with `list()` if you need two passes.
**Decorators without `functools.wraps`**, which break names in tracebacks and tests.
**Putting the cleanup after `yield` without `try/finally`** in a `@contextmanager`; an exception skips it.
**Treating hints as checks.** `x: int = "a"` runs without complaint.
**A giant class that does everything.** If a class has a name ending in `Manager` or `Handler` and 20 unrelated methods, split it by responsibility.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: A Stack class

task.text: Implement `class Stack` with `push(item)`, `pop()` (returns the most recently pushed item; raises `IndexError("pop from empty stack")` if empty), `peek()` (returns the top without removing it, same error when empty), `__len__`, and `__bool__` so an empty stack is falsy. Also give it a `__repr__` like `Stack([1, 2, 3])` with the oldest item first.

hints: Keep a list created in `__init__` (not in the class body), and use `append` and `pop`.

why.text: A stack is the structure behind undo, recursion and bracket matching. The list holds the data privately while the dunder methods give the class the feel of a built-in. Creating `_items` in `__init__` gives each stack its own list.

blocks.check:
s = Stack()
assert not s and len(s) == 0, "a new stack is empty and falsy"
s.push(1); s.push(2); s.push(3)
assert len(s) == 3 and s, "three items pushed"
assert repr(s) == "Stack([1, 2, 3])", f"repr was {s!r}"
assert s.peek() == 3 and len(s) == 3, "peek must not remove"
assert s.pop() == 3 and s.pop() == 2, "pop returns the newest first"
assert s.pop() == 1 and not s
for op in (s.pop, s.peek):
    try:
        op()
        raise AssertionError("empty stack should raise IndexError")
    except IndexError as e:
        assert str(e) == "pop from empty stack", f"message was {e}"

blocks.title: A Subnet with membership

task.text: Write `class Subnet` taking a CIDR string such as `"192.168.1.0/24"` (host bits allowed). It needs: `__contains__(address)` accepting an address string, returning `False` instead of raising for text that is not an IPv4 address; `__len__` returning the number of usable hosts (`pow(2, 32 - prefix) - 2`, but a /31 has 2 and a /32 has 1); `__iter__` yielding host addresses as strings; and `__repr__` like `Subnet('192.168.1.0/24')`.

hints: `ipaddress.IPv4Network(cidr, strict=False)` accepts an address with host bits set and rounds down.

why.text: The class wraps a library object and exposes exactly the protocol a collection needs. Callers write `ip in lan`, `len(lan)` and `for h in lan` and never touch the `ipaddress` API, which makes the model easy to change later.

blocks.check:
lan = Subnet("192.168.1.77/24")
assert repr(lan) == "Subnet('192.168.1.0/24')", f"repr was {lan!r}"
assert "192.168.1.200" in lan and "192.168.2.1" not in lan, "membership"
assert "not-an-ip" not in lan, "bad text must be False, not an exception"
assert len(lan) == 254, f"len was {len(lan)}"
assert len(Subnet("10.0.0.0/30")) == 2 and len(Subnet("10.0.0.0/31")) == 2 and len(Subnet("10.0.0.5/32")) == 1
assert list(Subnet("192.0.2.0/30")) == ["192.0.2.1", "192.0.2.2"], "iteration yields host strings"

blocks.title: A timing decorator

task.text: Write a decorator `timed` that records how long each call to the wrapped function took, in seconds, in the attribute `last_duration` of the wrapper function (a float), returns the function's result unchanged, and preserves the function's name and docstring. Use `time.perf_counter()`.

hints: Three layers are not needed here: `timed` takes the function and returns the wrapper.
Put the timing in `try/finally` so the duration is recorded even if the function raises.

why.text: Storing the duration on the wrapper is a simple way to expose a measurement without printing. `try/finally` records it on errors too, `*args, **kwargs` lets it wrap any signature, and `wraps` keeps the metadata.

blocks.title: A lazy log reader

task.text: Write a generator function `parse_log(lines)` that takes an iterable of access-log lines and **yields** one dict `{"ip": ..., "status": int}` per valid line. A valid line has the IP as its first word and a three-digit status code as the first word after the second double quote. Skip invalid lines silently. It must be lazy: it must not read more of the input than needed to produce the item being requested.

hints: A `for` loop over `lines` with a `yield` inside makes the function a generator. `continue` skips bad lines.
`line.split('"')[2].split()[0]` is the status field; check `isdigit()` before `int()`.

why.text: Because the function yields inside the loop, it pulls one input line per output item and never builds a list. The same function works on a file object, a list, or the output of another generator, which is exactly how shell stages combine.

blocks.check:
consumed = []
def source():
    for line in [
        '198.51.100.8 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:14:15 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 7625',
        'damaged line',
        '45.33.32.156 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:14:42 +0000] "GET /.env HTTP/1.1" 404 365',
        '172.16.5.9 - - [08/Oct/2026:09:15:02 +0000] "GET /x HTTP/1.1" 404 90',
    ]:
        consumed.append(line)
        yield line
g = parse_log(source())
assert iter(g) is g, "parse_log must be a generator"
first = next(g)
assert first == {"ip": "198.51.100.8", "status": 200}, f"first record was {first}"
assert len(consumed) == 1, f"read {len(consumed)} lines to produce one record; be lazy"
second = next(g)
assert second == {"ip": "45.33.32.156", "status": 404}, "damaged lines are skipped"
assert len(consumed) == 3
assert list(g) == [{"ip": "172.16.5.9", "status": 404}]

blocks.title: Fix the shared state

task.text: This `Host` class has a bug: every host seems to know the ports of every other host. Fix it without changing the method names or what they return, then make `Host` print as `Host('192.0.2.1', ports=[22])` using `__repr__`.

hints: Where is the list created, and how many times does that code run?

why.text: A list in the class body is created once, when the class statement runs, and every instance finds it through attribute lookup. Creating it in `__init__` runs once per instance.

blocks.check:
a, b = Host("192.0.2.1"), Host("192.0.2.2")
a.open(22)
assert b.ports == [], f"b should have no ports but has {b.ports}"
assert a.ports == [22]
assert repr(a) == "Host('192.0.2.1', ports=[22])", f"repr was {a!r}"

Start `python3 -i netmodel.py` and, at the prompt, create an `Inventory` with three hosts, record scan results for one of them, then try: `list(inv)`, `"10.0.0.5" in inv`, `len(inv)`, `Subnet("192.168.1.0/24")`, `inv["192.168.1.1"]`, and `vars(host)`. hints: `python3 -i` runs the file, then leaves you at the `>>>` prompt with all its names defined.
Press `Ctrl+D` to leave the Python prompt.

why.text: Objects are easiest to learn by interrogating them. `vars`, `dir`, `type` and `help` answer questions without reading the source, and changing a dunder method shows that syntax such as `len(x)` and `in` really dispatches to your code.

blocks.title: Inherit or compose?

task.text: For each design, decide between inheritance and composition and justify it in one sentence: (1) `Router` and `Switch` both need `ip`, `name` and `describe()`. (2) A `Scanner` needs to use either a TCP probe or an ICMP probe. (3) An `Inventory` needs a list of `Host` objects. (4) `LoggingInventory` should behave exactly like `Inventory` but also log each `add`.

blocks.solution: 1. Inheritance from a `Device` base class: both are devices and share most behavior. 2. Composition: pass the probe object to the scanner; the relationship is "uses", and you can swap probes. 3. Composition: an inventory has hosts, it is not a kind of host (or of list). 4. Inheritance is reasonable (a subclass overriding `add` and calling `super().add`), though composition (wrapping an inventory) is safer if `Inventory` is likely to change.

why.text: The is-a / has-a test settles most cases, and the second question to ask is whether you will want to replace the part at run time (composition) or extend a stable base (inheritance).

questions.q: What does `h.ping()` do when `ping` is defined as `def ping(self)` on class `Host`?

options.text: Copies `h` and calls `ping` on the copy

questions.why: A method is a function on the class; accessing it through an instance binds the instance as the first argument.

questions.q: You define `__eq__` on a class and nothing else. What happens when you put an instance in a set?

options.text: A `TypeError: unhashable type`, because defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None
The set silently ignores the item

questions.why: Python removes the default hash when you define `__eq__` so that equal objects cannot get unequal hashes. Define `__hash__` as well for immutable data.

questions.q: Which dunder method does `x in obj` call first?
questions.why: `in` calls `__contains__`; if it is missing Python falls back to iterating with `__iter__` and then to `__getitem__`.

questions.q: What does this print? `g = (n * 2 for n in range(3)); print(list(g), list(g))`
questions.why: A generator expression produces its values once; the second `list(g)` finds it exhausted.

options.text: It makes the wrapper run faster
It lets the decorator accept arguments
It copies the wrapped function's name and docstring onto the wrapper so tracebacks and `help()` show the real function
It prevents the wrapped function from raising

questions.why: Without it every decorated function appears as `wrapper`, which confuses logs, debuggers and test reports.

questions.q: What is true of `def f(x: int) -> str` when you call `f("a")` and it returns something that is not a str?

options.text: Python raises TypeError before running the body
Python runs it normally; a type checker or editor inspection would flag it
The annotation converts the argument to int

questions.why: Annotations are metadata. Only tools such as mypy, pyright and PyCharm check them.

blocks.text: Project: netmodel, the object model for netkit

blocks.title: netmodel.py, hosts, ports, subnets and an inventory

blocks.text: The capstone merges your shell and Python tools into `netkit`. Everything it reports (a scan, a ping run, a DNS lookup) is about the same few things: hosts, ports, scan results, subnets. This module defines them once, with validation at the boundary and a small, consistent API, so later chapters add behavior instead of re-inventing data structures.
The design choices, each from this chapter:

items.text: **`PortState`** is an `Enum` so a state can never be a misspelled string.
**`Port`** is a frozen, ordered dataclass: immutable (usable as a dict key), sortable, validated in `__post_init__`, with a `parse` class method and a short `__str__`.
**`ScanResult`** is a plain dataclass with an `is_open` property.
**`Host`** is an ordered dataclass keyed by IP (`compare=False` on everything else) holding its results; `open_ports` is a property.
**`Subnet`** is a regular class with dunder methods, so it behaves as a collection of host addresses.
**`Inventory`** composes hosts in a dict, iterates in address order and exposes generator methods (`in_subnet`, `open_ports`).

blocks.text: Step 1: The module

`Subnet.__contains__` and `Inventory.__contains__` accept either an address string or a `Host`: `getattr(item, "ip", item)` uses the `ip` attribute if the object has one and otherwise the item itself, which is duck typing in one line.

blocks.text: Step 3: Tests
Create a virtual environment (`python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && python3 -m pip install pytest`) and save the tests next to the module:

blocks.code:
import pytest

from netmodel import Host, Inventory, Port, PortState, ScanResult, Subnet


def test_port_validates_and_parses():
    assert Port.parse("53/udp") == Port(53, "udp")
    assert str(Port(443)) == "443/tcp"
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        Port(0)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        Port(80, "icmp")


def test_ports_sort_by_number_then_protocol():
    assert sorted([Port(443), Port(22), Port(22, "udp")]) == [Port(22), Port(22, "udp"), Port(443)]


def test_host_records_open_ports_only():
    h = Host("192.0.2.5")
    h.record(ScanResult(Port(22), PortState.OPEN))
    h.record(ScanResult(Port(23), PortState.CLOSED))
    assert h.open_ports == [Port(22)]


def test_subnet_behaves_like_a_collection():
    lan = Subnet("192.168.1.0/24")
    assert len(lan) == 254
    assert "192.168.1.200" in lan and "192.168.2.1" not in lan
    assert "not-an-ip" not in lan
    assert str(next(iter(lan))) == "192.168.1.1"


def test_inventory_iterates_in_address_order():
    inv = Inventory([Host("192.168.1.20"), Host("10.0.0.5"), Host("192.168.1.1")])
    assert [str(h.ip) for h in inv] == ["10.0.0.5", "192.168.1.1", "192.168.1.20"]
    assert "10.0.0.5" in inv and len(inv) == 3


def test_inventory_rejects_duplicates():
    inv = Inventory([Host("10.0.0.5")])
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="duplicate"):
        inv.add(Host("10.0.0.5"))

blocks.text: Step 4: Extend it
Choose at least two:

items.text: Add `Host.from_line("192.168.1.1 router 22/tcp,80/tcp")` as a class method that parses a line from a hosts file.
Give `Inventory` a `from_json` class method that reads back what `to_json` wrote, and a test that round-trips it.
Make `Subnet.__iter__` skip any address that is in a set of reserved hosts passed to the constructor.
Add `ScanResult.__str__` and a `PortState` method `symbol()` returning `+`, `-` or `?`, then print a one-line-per-port report.
Write a generator `slow_hosts(inv, threshold_ms)` that yields hosts having any result slower than the threshold.

blocks.text: In [Python networking](#py-net) the real probes (sockets, ICMP through `subprocess`) will produce `ScanResult`s for this model, and the capstone `netkit` reads and writes the JSON that `Inventory.to_json` defines.
Next: [Python networking](#py-net) puts these models to work: sockets, a port scanner, parallel probes with threads, and parsing real network data into `Host` and `ScanResult` objects.

terms.def: A blueprint that defines the attributes and methods of a type
One object created from a class
The first parameter of an instance method; the object the method was called on
A name attached to an object or class, accessed with a dot
A function defined in a class that receives the instance (or class) as its first argument
A special method with double underscores on both sides, called by Python syntax and built-ins (__len__, __iter__)
An attribute whose reads and writes run methods, used for validation and computed values
A class decorated with @dataclass so that __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ are generated from annotated fields
A subclass receiving the attributes and methods of a parent class
Method resolution order: the sequence of classes Python searches for an attribute or super() call
Building an object from other objects it holds and uses, instead of inheriting from them
Accepting any object that has the needed methods, without checking its class
An object that returns one item per next() call and raises StopIteration at the end
An iterator written as a function with yield, which pauses and resumes between values
A function that takes a function and returns a replacement, applied with the @ syntax
An object with __enter__ and __exit__ that a with statement uses for setup and guaranteed cleanup
An annotation of the expected type, read by editors and checkers but not enforced by Python
